items.title: Pneumothorax — film taken in expiration
items.caption: A real chest film of a pneumothorax taken in expiration. Breathing out shrinks the lung but not the pleural air, so the edge of the lung stands out.
look: A thin white line — the edge of the lung — separate from the chest wall
No lung markings between that line and the chest wall
The other side: markings reach the periphery
Mediastinum and trachea: pushed away from the air means tension
teach: Most pneumothoraces show on an ordinary inspiratory film; an expiratory film is not routine.
Tension is a clinical diagnosis — a crashing patient gets decompressed, not a film.
Skin folds and the scapula edge mimic a pleural line: lung markings continue past a fold, not past the lung edge.

quiz.q: Which sign confirms the pneumothorax on this film?
options: A thin lung-edge line with no lung markings beyond it
One hemithorax whiter than the other
quiz.explain: The visceral pleura (edge of the lung) seen as a line, with black, markingless air between it and the chest wall, is the sign. Blunting suggests fluid; a white hemithorax suggests fluid, collapse or consolidation.

items.title: Positive FAST — right upper quadrant
items.caption: A real hepatorenal (RUQ) view from a trauma FAST: a black, anechoic stripe of free fluid between the liver and the right kidney in Morison’s pouch.
look: Morison’s pouch — the potential space between them
A black (anechoic) stripe of free fluid in that space
teach: Supine, Morison’s pouch is the lowest upper-abdominal space, so fluid gathers there first.
In an unstable trauma patient a positive FAST points to the abdomen as the bleeding source — theatre or angiography.
A negative FAST does not rule out injury: small volumes and retroperitoneal bleeding are missed. Repeat it when things change.
Clotted blood can look grey rather than black.

quiz.q: What is the black stripe between liver and kidney?
options: Free intraperitoneal fluid in Morison’s pouch
quiz.explain: Fluid is anechoic (black). Between liver and kidney it sits in the hepatorenal recess — in trauma, blood until proven otherwise. Rib shadows are black bands that run from the probe straight down through everything.

items.finding: IVC traced into the right atrium
items.title: IVC — long axis into the right atrium
items.caption: A real subcostal long-axis scan following the inferior vena cava through the liver into the right atrium.
look: The IVC running into the right atrium (cavo-atrial junction)
A hepatic vein joining near the junction
teach: Prove it is the IVC by following it into the right atrium — the aorta lies deeper and to the left and never enters the heart.
Measure 1–2 cm below the hepatic-vein junction, at right angles to the vessel.
Small and collapsing fits a low right-atrial pressure; wide and fixed fits a high one.
It does not reliably predict who will respond to fluid: positive-pressure ventilation, raised abdominal pressure, RV failure, tricuspid regurgitation and vigorous breathing all change it.
Read it with the lungs, the heart, the patient and the trend — never alone.

quiz.q: A wide IVC that barely changes with breathing most directly tells you…
options: The patient will respond to a fluid bolus
quiz.explain: IVC size reflects right-atrial pressure. That can be high from volume, RV failure, tamponade, tricuspid regurgitation or positive pressure — it is not a verdict on fluid responsiveness.

items.title: Internal jugular vein — compressibility
items.caption: A real neck scan of the internal jugular vein and carotid artery: the vein collapses under probe pressure while the artery stays round.
look: Internal jugular vein — larger, thin-walled, oval
The vein collapses with gentle pressure; the artery does not
How the two lie: the vein lateral and superficial, often overlapping the artery
teach: Compressibility, shape and wall thickness identify the vein — confirm with a steady compression, not a glance.
Doppler colour shows direction relative to the probe, not artery or vein: red and blue alone prove nothing.
Veins can look pulsatile from transmitted pulsation; an artery still will not collapse.
Where the vein sits over the artery, a needle through both walls reaches the carotid — keep the tip in view.
A collapsing IJ in a hypovolaemic patient is a small target; head-down tilt fills it.

quiz.q: Which finding best identifies the vein?
options: It collapses completely with gentle probe pressure
It shows blue on colour Doppler
quiz.explain: Veins collapse under light pressure; arteries do not. Colour depends on flow direction relative to the probe, veins can pulsate, and depth varies between people.
